report.currency: USD (market reports in USD; tables in $ millions unless stated)
report.verdict: Tennessee's mobile-only sportsbook market took $591.9m of gross wagers in September 2026 (+4.7% YoY; taxable gross handle $588.6m, +4.9%) — the best month of 2026 but still short of the $598.6m booked in November 2024 — and yielded $10.88m of privilege tax under the only handle-based regime in the US (1.85% of gross handle). Growth has decelerated hard from the World Cup-inflated summer (+30–38% YoY in June/July) to mid-single digits, the licensed field has thinned to nine operators, and the regulatory story is now enforcement-led (a Sixth Circuit ruling that Tennessee's Sports Gaming Act reaches Kalshi's sports contracts, and a run of offshore cease-and-desists) rather than tax or licensing change. For an entrant, Tennessee is cheap to enter but structurally rewards scale and high-hold product; it penalises promo-heavy or low-margin models because free bets are taxed at face value.

kpis.label: Tax regime
kpis.delta: Unchanged since 1 Jul 2023; fed. 0.25% excise deductible

summary: **Single-product, mobile-only market.** Tennessee permits online sports wagering and regulated paid fantasy only — no commercial or tribal casinos, no retail sportsbooks, no iGaming; the Tennessee Education Lottery and limited charitable gaming complete the legal perimeter. Online penetration of sports betting is therefore 100% by construction. Regulator: the Tennessee Sports Wagering Council (SWC), independent since 1 Jan 2022 (Public Chapter 593) and responsible for fantasy sports since 1 Jul 2023.

**September 2026 print: $591.9m gross wagers (+4.7% YoY vs $565.3m), gross handle $588.6m (+4.9%), privilege tax $10.88m (+4.9% vs $10.4m).** Adjustments (voids, cancellations, negative resettlements) were ≈$3.3m, 0.56% of wagers. Month-on-month, wagers jumped +42.8% as NFL and college football restarted.

**Best month of 2026 — but the peak has plateaued.** September's $591.9m remains below the $598.6m of gross wagers recorded in November 2024 (SWC), and December 2024 was $572.7m; football-season months have sat in a ~$550–600m band for two years. The 2022–26 September CAGR of 15.1% ($336.9m → $591.9m) flatters a market whose recent organic growth is mid-single digit.

**Sharp deceleration from a World Cup summer.** Gross handle grew +30% in June 2026 ($456.1m, World Cup opening month), +38% in July ($412.1m vs $298.0m) and +10.7% in August ($412.0m vs $372.3m) before slowing to +4.9% in September. Q3-26 gross wagers ≈$1.42bn vs ≈$1.24bn in Q3-25 (+~15%), roughly two-thirds of it tournament-driven.

**Annual scale: CY2025 handle $5.87bn (+10.8%), tax $107.6m; FY2026 (Jul-25–Jun-26) handle ≈$6.0bn [secondary]; 2026 YTD Jan–Sep ≈$4.37bn.** That is ≈$1,100 of handle per 21+ adult per year (approx.), in line with mature US online-only states.

**No GGR is published — and the 'hold' figures in circulation are artefacts.** Since 1 Jul 2023 the SWC reports only gross wagers, adjustments, gross handle and tax (its FAQ states payouts/AGI are no longer collected for tax purposes). Trade trackers' Tennessee 'AGI' and 'hold' (e.g. $37.9m / 9.19% for July 2026) are simply tax ÷ 20% and 1.85% ÷ 20%, not operator data. Independent GGR estimates for 2025 range from $0.62bn (Track360) to $700.2m (AGA, which applies a Tennessee hold premium); the last actual disclosures were Sept–Nov 2022 holds of 12.9%, 8.6% and 10.3% under the old 10%-minimum-hold regime.

**Tax regime: 1.85% privilege tax on gross handle, with the 0.25% federal excise deductible (PC 450, effective 1 Jul 2023).** Gross handle = gross wagers including promotional wagers, less cancelled/voided wagers and negative resettlements — there is no promo deduction, so free bets are taxed at face value. It replaced a 20%-of-AGI tax plus a 10% minimum-hold rule (operators under 10% hold paid the shortfall or a $25,000 fine). Effective burden ≈20.6% of GGR at 9% hold, 26.4% at 7%, 14.2% at 13%. Sept-26 implied rate on gross handle: 1.85%.

**Tax distribution is politically entrenched:** 80% to the Lottery for Education Account, 15% to local governments, 5% to the Department of Mental Health for problem-gambling services (≈$5.4m in CY2025). This makes a rate cut improbable and a rate rise a live, if unproposed, option as other states (NJ, IL, MD, LA) have raised sports-betting taxes in 2025–26.

**Licensing: uncapped licences, no casino tether, $50,000 non-refundable application fee and a $750,000 annual fee for operators with ≥$100m gross wagers in the prior 12 months** (lower tier for smaller books — reportedly $375,000 [unverified]). PC 450 also created vendor registration and capped administrative fines at $25,000 per violation. Any suitable operator can apply directly — unusual in the US, where most states require a land-based partner.

**Operator landscape is consolidating: 12 licensed sportsbooks at end-2024 → 10 at end-2025 (AGA) → 9 on the SWC register at 23 Sep 2026; 16 registered fantasy operators.** The SWC publishes no operator-level handle, so Tennessee market shares are n/a; national patterns imply a FanDuel/DraftKings duopoly of ~70%+ of online handle [unverified for TN].

**Fixed-cost squeeze explains the exits.** A $750k annual fee is 8.3% of GGR for a $100m-handle book at 9% hold but 0.8% for a $1bn book; add 1.85% handle tax (20.6% of GGR) and 0.25% federal excise (2.8%), and all-in government take runs ≈26% of GGR for a $300m-handle operator versus ≈24% for a $1bn one — and 34%+ for a low-hold entrant at 7%.

**Enforcement has become the regulator's headline activity.** The SWC reported on 9 Sep 2026 that a cease-and-desist had shut another illegal sportsbook, and on 30 Sep issued C&Ds to Sportbet and FullStarSportsbook (announced 7 Oct), framing the eradication of illegal books as a core mission.

**Prediction markets: on 25 Sep 2026 the Sixth Circuit held that Tennessee's sports gaming law can be applied to Kalshi's sports event contracts and vacated the district court's preliminary injunction** (the injunction stays in force until the mandate issues). This is the most important regulatory development of the period for licensed operators' channelisation; it remains subject to en banc/certiorari risk.

**Payments are standard US rails** (debit, ACH/online banking, e-wallets, prepaid), with credit-card funding prohibited in Tennessee [statutory basis to confirm]; no mobile-money dimension; 21+ with geolocation/KYC. Tennessee levies no state income tax on winnings (Hall tax fully repealed 2021), but the federal OBBBA caps gambling-loss deductions at 90% from tax year 2026 — a headwind for high-volume bettors that could push sharp handle offshore or into prediction markets.

**Responsible gambling and advertising rules are mid-pack, not outliers.** Statutory self-exclusion for sports wagering and fantasy (weekly licensee list transmission, monthly reporting), 5% of tax ring-fenced for treatment, TN REDLINE helpline, and advertising standards under SWC Rule 1350-01 (RG messaging, no targeting of under-21s) [detail not re-verified]. No 2026 Tennessee advertising-restriction legislation was identified.

**Direction of travel: enforcement-led, fiscally stable, structurally closed to casino/iGaming.** No proposal to change the 1.85% rate, fee tiers or licence structure was identified in 2026; the 2027 General Assembly (convenes January) is the watch point for prediction-market, sweepstakes and any tax tinkering. Tennessee's handle tax is being showcased in-state as a stability model (September: TN tax +4.9% while New Jersey's fell 17.7% on low hold).

**Fiscal outlook:** FY2027 Q1 (Jul–Sep 2026) privilege tax ≈$26.1m (+~14% vs $22.8m; August estimated) and CY2026E tax ≈$113–115m (+5–7%) — estimates. Absent a World Cup, 2027 handle growth should revert to +4–7% unless prediction-market enforcement or OBBBA behaviour shifts materially change channelisation.

**Read-through for B2Tech:** Tennessee is a low-friction, low-fixed-cost licence (≈$0.8m year-1 fees) with no gatekeeper partner, but the handle tax structurally favours a scaled, high-hold, parlay-led product and penalises a promo-led land-grab (bonus handle taxed at 1.85%). A realistic challenger share of 2–5% equates to ≈$120–300m annual handle, or ≈$11–27m GGR at 9% hold (illustrative), against ≈$3.0–7.3m of tax, excise and fees. Entry only makes sense as part of a multi-state US footprint with existing content, trading and risk infrastructure.

segments.name: Online sports betting — volume, seasonality and trend
segments.headline: September's $591.9m is the best month of 2026, but growth has slowed to +4.9% and peak-season handle has plateaued below the Nov-2024 high.
narrative: The SWC's September 2026 Monthly Sports Gaming Report shows $591.9m of gross wagers, ≈$3.3m of adjustments (voided and cancelled wagers plus negative resettlements, 0.56% of wagers) and $588.6m of gross handle, on which $10.88m of privilege tax was assessed. Against September 2025 ($565.3m gross wagers, $10.4m tax) that is +4.7% on wagers, +4.9% on the taxable base and +4.9% on tax — the three figures move together because the levy is a flat percentage of handle. Month-on-month, wagers rose 42.8% from August's $414.5m as the NFL and SEC football calendars resumed; September is typically the third- or fourth-largest month of the Tennessee year behind November, December and January.

The longer series shows a market whose peak months have stopped growing. September gross wagers rose from $336.9m (2022) to $445.2m-era levels in late 2023, $565.3m (2025) and $591.9m (2026) — a 15.1% four-year CAGR — yet the highest month the SWC has published remains November 2024 at $598.6m, with December 2024 at $572.7m. By contrast March 2026 gross wagers of $562.6m were +18.8% on March 2024 ($473.6m): off-peak months are growing faster than the football peak, consistent with product-led engagement gains (same-game parlays, in-play, basketball/baseball depth) rather than new-bettor adoption, which appears close to saturation in a state of ~5.4m adults.

Summer 2026 was tournament-inflated and should not be extrapolated. Gross handle was $456.1m in June (+30% YoY, the FIFA World Cup's opening month on US soil), ≈$412.1m in July (+38% against $298.0m) and $412.0m in August (+10.7% against $372.3m), before September's +4.9%. Q3-26 gross wagers were ≈$1.42bn versus ≈$1.24bn in Q3-25 (+~15%); stripping out the July–August tournament tail, the underlying run-rate is mid-to-high single digits, and September — a clean football-only comparison — is the most reliable read of trend.

Tennessee does not report GGR, payouts or hold. The SWC's FAQ explains that since the 1 Jul 2023 switch to a handle tax it no longer collects or publishes payouts/AGI. Figures labelled 'GGR' or 'hold' for Tennessee in trade trackers are tax ÷ 20% (giving an invariant ~9.2% 'hold' every month) and must not be used for margin benchmarking. The last genuine disclosures were September–November 2022 (hold 12.9%, 8.6%, 10.3% on $336.9m, $405.3m and $439.5m of wagers) under the old 10% minimum-hold regime. The AGA estimates 2025 GGR at $700.2m (+22%), implying ~11.9% hold; Track360 puts it at $0.62bn (~10.6%). On $588.6m of September handle, GGR at 9–11% hold would be $53–65m — an estimate, not a reported figure.

Channel mix is trivial but important: 100% of handle is mobile/online; there are no retail books, kiosks or casinos, so the market has none of the retail-to-online migration tailwind that still flatters many US states, and no land-based cross-sell. Handle per 21+ adult is ≈$110 for September and ≈$1,100 for CY2025 (approx.), comparable to mature online-first states, which supports the saturation reading.

For an entrant the implication is that Tennessee is a share-capture market, not an expansion market: assume underlying handle growth of +4–7% a year, episodic event spikes, and incremental volume coming from channelisation (offshore books and prediction markets being pushed out) rather than first-time bettors. Product depth in parlays and in-play — the drivers of off-peak growth — is where share is contested.

segments.name: Tax regime and the state's fiscal take
segments.headline: A flat 1.85% of handle (≈20.6% of GGR at 9% hold) that shifts all hold risk to operators, taxes promotional wagers at face value, and has been stable since July 2023.
narrative: Public Chapter 450 (2023), effective 1 Jul 2023, replaced Tennessee's original 20% tax on adjusted gross income with a 1.85% privilege tax on gross handle. The General Assembly's Fiscal Review Committee memorandum records that the bill as introduced proposed 2% and was enacted at 1.85%, and that licensees may deduct federal excise tax paid (0.25% of wagers) from gross handle. Gross handle is defined as gross wagers — including promotional or free-bet wagers — less cancelled and voided wagers and negative resettlements. September 2026's $10.88m on $588.6m is 1.85% of gross handle, consistent with the formula.

The previous regime also carried a 10% minimum-hold rule: an operator whose monthly hold fell below 10% had to pay the privilege tax as if it had achieved 10% or a $25,000 penalty. The SWC's FAQ notes the old structure was 'mathematically equivalent' to about 2% of handle, which is why the 1.85% rate was broadly revenue-neutral for the state while removing the hold floor and the burden of auditing payouts. The Comptroller's May 2024 performance audit confirmed operators must hold privilege-tax funds in a segregated account pending monthly transfer.

Fiscally the model is delivering steady growth: CY2025 collections were $107.6m on $5.87bn of handle (1.83% of wagers); FY2026 Q1 (Jul–Sep 2025) was $22.8m versus $21.0m a year earlier; FY2027 Q1 (Jul–Sep 2026) is ≈$26.1m (+~14%), comprising $7.59m in July, ≈$7.6m in August (estimated) and $10.88m in September. Proceeds are split 80% to the Lottery for Education Account, 15% to local governments and 5% to the Department of Mental Health and Substance Abuse Services for problem-gambling programmes. In-state commentary contrasts Tennessee's +4.9% September tax with New Jersey's −17.7% on a low-hold month — the handle tax is being showcased as a stability model, which entrenches it politically.

The economic incidence is what matters for an operator. Because the tax is hold-agnostic, every point of hold moves the GGR-equivalent rate: 26.4% at 7%, 20.6% at 9%, 16.8% at 11%, 14.2% at 13%. Add the 0.25% federal excise (2.8% of GGR at 9% hold) and a $750,000 annual fee (2.8% of GGR on $300m of handle; 8.3% on $100m), and the all-in government take is ≈26% of GGR for a $300m-handle book, ≈24% for a $1bn book and ≈34% for a low-hold $300m entrant. Two features are hostile to challengers: there is no deduction for promotional wagers (a $100 free bet costs $1.85 of tax before any customer value is created, unlike the promo deductions in Michigan, Pennsylvania or Colorado), and sharp-friendly, low-margin pricing is penalised rather than rewarded.

Peer context: at ~20% of GGR-equivalent Tennessee sits between New Jersey/Ohio (around 20%) and Pennsylvania/New York (36%/51%), and has not moved while several states raised rates in 2025–26 (New Jersey, Illinois, Maryland, Louisiana). A hypothetical move to 2.0% of handle — the figure originally tabled in 2023 — would add ≈$9m a year at current volumes; no such proposal was identified in 2026, but the national direction makes it a non-trivial tail risk for 2027 budget season.

Modelling guidance: treat Tennessee as 1.85% of gross handle + 0.25% of wagers (federal) + $0.75m fixed, with promotional handle fully taxable. For a 9%-hold product this is ≈23.4% of GGR before the fee; for a 12%-hold parlay-led product it is ≈17.5% — the structural advantage of the national leaders' product mix is amplified by the tax base.

segments.name: Licensing, operator landscape and the wider gambling perimeter
segments.headline: Uncapped, untethered licences at $50k + $750k a year — cheap to enter, but a shrinking field (12 → 10 → 9) shows sub-scale economics do not work under a handle tax.
narrative: The legal basis is the Tennessee Sports Gaming Act (HB 1, 2019), which made Tennessee the first US state to legalise sports betting with no pre-existing casino industry; wagering went live on 1 Nov 2020 under the Lottery's Sports Wagering Advisory Council. Public Chapter 593 created the independent Sports Wagering Council from 1 Jan 2022; PC 450 (2023) rewrote the tax and fee structure; and the Fantasy Sports Act was transferred to the SWC from 1 Jul 2023. Operating rules sit in Chapter 1350-01. The regulator's monthly report, published around the third week of the following month, is the only official market statistic; from June 2026 the files carry a '(UA)' suffix, which we read as unaudited/subject to revision [interpretation].

Licence economics are simple and, by US standards, open. There is no cap on the number of sports gaming operator licences and — because Tennessee has no casinos or racetracks — no requirement for a land-based market-access partner, which elsewhere costs entrants a revenue share or seven-figure access fee. The application fee is $50,000, non-refundable. Under PC 450 the annual fee is $750,000 for licensees with ≥$100m of gross wagers in the preceding 12 months, with a lower tier for smaller operators (reportedly $375,000) [unverified]; before July 2023 every operator paid a flat $750,000 ($50k + $700k renewal). PC 450 also introduced vendor registration for suppliers, key-personnel licensing continues, and administrative fines are capped at $25,000 per violation.

The field is consolidating. The AGA counts 12 live online sportsbooks at end-2024 and 10 at end-2025; the SWC's register showed 9 on 23 Sep 2026. The SWC does not publish operator-level handle or tax, so Tennessee market shares cannot be verified; national data suggest FanDuel and DraftKings hold ~70%+ of US online handle between them, with BetMGM, Caesars, Fanatics, bet365 and Hard Rock Bet forming the next tier [unverified for TN]. The exits have come from the long tail — regional and start-up brands for whom a $750k fee plus a tax that ignores margin pushed government take above 30% of GGR.

Compliance architecture, per SWC Rule 1350-01 and the Comptroller's audit: monthly transfer of privilege tax and a report of gross wagers, deductions and gross handle by the fifth business day; a segregated account for tax funds; weekly transmission of the licensee-specific self-exclusion list and a monthly self-exclusion report; key-personnel suitability; and — under the 2019 Act — use of official league data for in-play (Tier 2) wagers, Tennessee having been the first state to mandate it [current rule wording to confirm]. Minimum age is 21 and geolocation/KYC are standard.

The wider perimeter is narrow and likely to stay so. There are no commercial or tribal casinos, no retail sportsbooks, no iGaming and no live proposal for any of them; casino gambling would require constitutional change. The Tennessee Education Lottery (draw and instant games) and limited charitable gaming are the only other legal verticals, and 16 fantasy operators (DFS and pick'em) are registered with the SWC. Prediction markets are the contested frontier (see enforcement).

For B2Tech the entry maths are: ≈$0.8m of government fees in year one, no partner tax, a nine-operator field with an exiting tail — but a tax base that makes bonus-led acquisition expensive. A challenger needs to reach ≥$100–150m of annual handle quickly to keep fixed government costs under 10% of GGR, and should target share from the exiting tail and from channelised offshore/prediction-market volume rather than from the duopoly.

segments.name: Enforcement, prediction markets and political direction
segments.headline: The regulator's energy is on channelisation: a Sixth Circuit win over Kalshi's sports contracts and three offshore cease-and-desists in September alone; no tax or licensing change is on the table.
narrative: September 2026 was the SWC's most active enforcement month on record in public terms. On 9 Sep it announced that a cease-and-desist demand had forced another unlicensed sportsbook to stop serving Tennessee; on 30 Sep it issued C&Ds to two more, Sportbet and FullStarSportsbook (announced 7 Oct). The Council's stated mission now explicitly includes eradicating illegal sportsbooks and their supporting ecosystem — payment processors, affiliates and advertisers — which is where the next phase of pressure is likely to fall.

The prediction-market front moved decisively. On 25 Sep 2026 the US Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit held that Tennessee's sports gaming law can be applied to Kalshi's sports event contracts and vacated the preliminary injunction that had been shielding Kalshi from state enforcement; the injunction remains in force only until the court's mandate issues. If the mandate issues without en banc rehearing or a Supreme Court stay, the SWC gains a clear path to act against sports contracts offered by Kalshi — and, by extension, by Robinhood, Crypto.com and other CFTC-registered venues distributing them — to Tennessee residents. For licensed operators this is the single most material development of the period: sports contracts on prediction markets carry no state tax, no $750k fee and no 21+ or RG regime, and have been the fastest-growing untaxed competitor to regulated books through 2025–26.

Fiscal politics are stable. The handle tax is being promoted in-state as a model of revenue predictability, 80% of proceeds flow to education, and no bill to alter the 1.85% rate or fee tiers was identified in the 2026 session. The risks are second-order: a national wave of sports-betting tax increases (Illinois, New Jersey, Maryland, Louisiana) gives any future Tennessee budget-writer a template, and because the tax is on handle, any stall in volume shows straight through to receipts — a 2% rate was already on the table in 2023.

Governance and transparency are the weak points. Tennessee's monthly disclosure is thinner than most US states: no GGR, no operator-level data, no promotional spend, and no breakdown by sport or bet type. The Comptroller's 2024 performance audit covered the tax transition and controls rather than market transparency, and the June–September 2026 reports now carry an unexplained '(UA)' label. Operators and investors therefore depend on national proxies to benchmark Tennessee margins.

The political calendar to watch is the 2027 General Assembly (convenes January) — the natural venue for a prediction-market or sweepstakes-casino bill (both national trends), any advertising restriction, and any revisiting of fees or rate — following the November 2026 gubernatorial election and a January 2027 transition in the governor's office [election outcome not verified here]. Tennessee remains structurally closed to casino and iGaming expansion.

Net assessment for an entrant: regulatory risk is low-to-moderate and asymmetric — the probability-weighted downside is a modest tax increase, not a product or licensing restriction — while the enforcement trajectory (offshore and prediction markets) is a tangible tailwind to licensed-channel handle in 2027.

segments.name: Payments, responsible gambling and advertising
segments.headline: Standard US rails with a credit-card ban, a mid-pack RG regime funded by 5% of tax, and player-level headwinds that are federal (OBBBA) rather than Tennessee-specific.
narrative: Payments run on the conventional US stack: debit cards, ACH/online banking, PayPal/Venmo-type wallets and prepaid cards for deposits; ACH and wallet for withdrawals. Tennessee prohibits funding wagering accounts with credit cards — one of a handful of states (with Iowa and Massachusetts) to do so [statutory/rule basis to confirm]. There is no mobile-money dimension and no cash-at-retail network comparable to casino-state cages (third-party cash-voucher services may be offered; not verified). Processing costs are in the industry-normal 1.5–3% of deposits; the credit ban trims deposit conversion slightly but lowers chargeback and AML exposure.

Responsible gambling is statutory and SWC-administered. A statewide self-exclusion programme covers sports wagering and, since 2023, fantasy sports; licensees must transmit their licensee-specific self-exclusion list weekly and file a monthly self-exclusion report (Rule 1350-01-.07). Five per cent of privilege tax (≈$5.4m in CY2025, ≈$0.54m in September 2026 alone) is ring-fenced for the Department of Mental Health and Substance Abuse Services' problem-gambling programmes, and the TN REDLINE helpline is the mandated referral point. Deposit, wager and time limits and cooling-off tools are standard across licensees.

Advertising is governed by SWC Rule 1350-01 standards — responsible-gambling messaging, no targeting of persons under 21, no misleading inducement language — rather than by the volume or time-of-day restrictions seen in Ontario or parts of Europe [rule detail not re-verified]. No Tennessee advertising-restriction legislation was identified in 2026; the swing factor is federal (periodic SAFE Bet Act-style proposals) rather than state.

Player taxation moved against heavy bettors in 2026, but federally. Tennessee has no personal income tax on wagering winnings (the Hall tax was fully repealed from 2021) — a mild positive versus high-income-tax states — but the federal One Big Beautiful Bill Act caps gambling-loss deductions at 90% from tax year 2026, meaning a break-even high-volume bettor incurs a tax bill on phantom income. The behavioural risk is that sharp and high-frequency handle migrates to offshore books or prediction markets, which is precisely the leakage the SWC's enforcement push and the Sixth Circuit ruling aim to shut off.

Commercially, Tennessee's RG and payments rules are not a cost outlier and impose no special product constraints beyond the credit ban; the compliance lift for an operator already live in other US states is incremental. The real 2026–27 shifts in player economics are federal and should be modelled as a modest drag on high-value-segment handle rather than as a Tennessee-specific risk.

highlights.text: Scale with a stable, predictable government take: $5.87bn of handle in 2025 (+10.8%) and ≈$4.37bn Jan–Sep 2026; the 1.85% handle tax has been unchanged since July 2023 while NJ, IL, MD and LA raised rates — Tennessee's fiscal model is being showcased in-state, lowering near-term rate-hike risk.

Open, untethered licensing: no cap on licences and no casino market-access partner required (none exist), so entry costs are ≈$0.8m of fees in year one with no revenue-share to a land-based gatekeeper — rare in the US.

A thinning field creates share to capture: 12 operators at end-2024 → 10 at end-2025 → 9 in Sept 2026; the exiting tail's handle is up for grabs by a well-capitalised challenger without the market having to grow.

Enforcement tailwind for licensed books: the Sixth Circuit's 25 Sep 2026 ruling that Tennessee's law reaches Kalshi's sports contracts (PI vacated pending mandate) plus three offshore cease-and-desists in September point to meaningful channelisation of untaxed volume back to licensees in 2027.

Handle-based tax rewards high-hold product: a parlay/SGP-led book at 12% hold pays ≈15.4% of GGR in state tax versus ≈26.4% for a 7%-hold book — a structural edge for operators with strong parlay pricing and risk management.

100% digital market with mature per-capita engagement (≈$1,100 handle per 21+ adult per year): no retail capex, no cannibalisation debates, and off-peak months (March 2026 +18.8% vs March 2024) still growing on product depth.

lowlights.text: The handle tax penalises entrants: promotional wagers are taxed at face value (no promo deduction), so a bonus-led acquisition campaign carries a 1.85% levy on every free-bet dollar before any customer value is earned; low-margin or sharp-friendly pricing is punished rather than rewarded.

Growth has decelerated to mid-single digits: +4.9% in September after World Cup-inflated +30–38% in June/July, and peak-season handle has plateaued below the $598.6m of Nov-2024 for two years — this is a share-capture market, not an expansion market.

Opaque market data: the SWC publishes no GGR, no hold, no operator-level handle and no promo spend; trade-tracker 'hold' figures (~9.2%) are tax ÷ 20% artefacts. An entrant cannot benchmark margins or size the duopoly's share from official data.

Fixed-cost burden favours incumbents: the $750k annual fee is 8.3% of GGR for a $100m-handle book at 9% hold vs 0.8% for a $1bn book; all-in government take exceeds 30% of GGR for a sub-scale, low-hold entrant — the exact profile that has been exiting.

Prediction-market competition is not yet closed off: Kalshi's injunction stays in force until the Sixth Circuit mandate issues, with en banc/certiorari risk and an unresolved federal CFTC pre-emption question; untaxed sports contracts keep siphoning volume in the interim.

Federal OBBBA caps gambling-loss deductions at 90% from tax year 2026, creating phantom taxable income for high-volume bettors — a leakage risk to offshore books and prediction markets concentrated in the highest-value segment.

Tax-rate tail risk in the 2027 session: a 2% rate was already tabled in 2023, 80% of proceeds fund education, and the national direction is upward; a move to 2% would add ≈$9m a year to the state and ≈8% to operators' state-tax bill.

forecast.intro: Nothing in the rulebook changed in September 2026 — the 1.85% handle tax, $50k/$750k fee structure and nine-operator field are as they were — but two things moved that matter more: the Sixth Circuit's 25 Sep ruling against Kalshi's sports contracts and the SWC's escalating offshore cease-and-desist campaign, both of which push untaxed volume back toward licensed books once the mandate issues. On the numbers, the tax take bridge from CY2025 to CY2026 is volume-driven: $107.6m in 2025 rises on ≈$4.37bn of Jan–Sep wagers (≈$80.6m assessed, derived) plus an estimated ≈$33m for Q4-26 on ~$1.8bn of handle (+~5% YoY), giving ≈$113–115m (+5–7%). Roughly $2.5m of the uplift is World Cup (June–July) and will not recur in 2027; the rest is underlying mid-single-digit growth.
forecast.view: **Handle: +4–7% in 2027 (estimate), with downside in June–July as World Cup comparatives roll off and upside of 2–4 points if the Kalshi mandate issues and the SWC enforces against prediction-market sports contracts in H1 2027.** We expect November 2026 to test the $598.6m Nov-2024 record for the first time; failure to clear it would confirm peak-season saturation. **Margin: unobservable from official data — model 9–11% hold with the tax at 1.85% of handle (≈17–21% of GGR) plus 0.25% federal excise and $0.75m fixed; all-in ≈24–27% of GGR for a $300m–$1bn book.** **Rules: the base case (≈70%) is no change to rate, fees or licensing in the 2027 session; the main tail risk (≈20–25%) is a rate increase toward 2.0% framed as education funding, worth ≈$9m a year; the probability of casino or iGaming legalisation is negligible.** **Operator count: more likely to fall to 8 than rise to 10 in the next 12 months absent a new national entrant; the SWC's register, not handle growth, is the best leading indicator of competitive intensity.** **State fiscal take: FY2027 (Jul-26–Jun-27) privilege tax ≈$112–116m (estimate), +3–5% on FY2026's ≈$111m-equivalent, with Q1 already +~14%.**
watch: Issuance of the Sixth Circuit mandate in Kalshi v. Tennessee and any en banc or Supreme Court stay petition; first SWC enforcement step against Kalshi/Robinhood/Crypto.com sports contracts thereafter.
October–December 2026 SWC monthly reports: whether YoY handle growth holds ≥5% through the NFL season and whether November clears the $598.6m Nov-2024 record.
2027 General Assembly (from January): any bill touching the 1.85% privilege tax, fee tiers, prediction markets, sweepstakes casinos or advertising; and the post-election governor's first budget.
SWC operator register: further exits below nine, or a new national entrant; any change to the '(UA)' labelling or resumption of GGR/operator-level disclosure.
Offshore enforcement escalation toward payment processors, affiliates and advertisers supporting unlicensed books, following the September C&Ds.
Early-2027 behavioural evidence of OBBBA's 90% loss-deduction cap on high-volume handle (Q1-27 YoY in the sharp-heavy March basketball window).
